title: Maximum Subarray With Equal Products
statement:
`nums` is an array of positive integers. Call a subarray (a contiguous, non-empty run of elements) *product equivalent* when the product of all its elements equals its least common multiple multiplied by its greatest common divisor.

Return the length of the longest product equivalent subarray of `nums`.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct approach recomputes the product, gcd and lcm of every subarray from scratch, which is O(n³). Instead, fix the left end and grow the subarray one element at a time: each new element updates a running product, gcd and lcm with a single gcd call.

The hint gives the bound that keeps this fast and safe. Every value is at most 10, so any lcm divides lcm(1, …, 10) = 2520 and any gcd is at most 10: the right-hand side never exceeds 25200. The product never shrinks as the subarray grows, because every value is at least 1, so once it passes 25200 no longer subarray from this left end can qualify.

A useful fact: any two numbers satisfy a · b = lcm · gcd, so every pair qualifies and the answer is at least 2. Three or more numbers qualify exactly when they are pairwise coprime.

## Approach

1. Set `limit = 2520 * 10` and `best = 0`.
2. For each `left`, reset `product = 1`, `curGcd = 0` (since gcd(0, x) = x) and `curLcm = 1`.
3. Move `right` from `left` to the end, multiplying `nums[right]` into `product`. If it passes `limit`, stop this left end.
4. Update `curGcd` with `gcd`, and `curLcm` as `curLcm / gcd(curLcm, x) * x`.
5. If `product === curLcm * curGcd`, the subarray qualifies: update `best` with its length `right - left + 1`.
6. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1]`. From `left = 0`, `[1, 2, 1]` has product 2, lcm 2 and gcd 1, so `best = 3`; adding the second 2 makes the product 4 while lcm · gcd stays 2, and no longer run from index 0 recovers. From `left = 2`, `[1, 2, 1, 1, 1]` again has product 2, lcm 2 and gcd 1, so `best = 5`. Later starts leave too few elements to beat it, so the answer is 5.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · log V) with V = 2520: at most n(n + 1)/2 steps, each with two gcd calls on small numbers.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- An overall gcd of 1 is not enough: `[6, 10, 9]` has gcd 1 and lcm 90 but product 540, so only its pairs count.
- A repeated value breaks a run: `[5, 1, 5]` has product 25 but lcm · gcd = 5.
- Without the early stop the product of 100 values can reach 10^100; in Java or C that overflows and can fake a match.
- Reset all three running values for every new `left`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gcd` | helper returning the gcd of two numbers |
| `limit` | largest possible lcm · gcd, 2520 · 10 |
| `best` | longest qualifying length so far |
| `left`, `right` | first and last index of the current subarray |
| `product` | product of `nums[left..right]` |
| `curGcd`, `curLcm` | gcd and lcm of `nums[left..right]` |

narration.2: Euclid's algorithm: the gcd of a and b equals the gcd of b and a mod b.
narration.4: No lcm can exceed 2520 and no gcd can exceed 10, so lcm times gcd is at most 25200.
narration.6: Try every left end of a subarray.
narration.7: Start an empty subarray: product 1, gcd 0 (gcd(0, x) = x) and lcm 1.

narration.11: Fold the new element into the product.
narration.12: The product only grows, so once it passes the limit no longer subarray from this left end can match.
narration.15: Fold the new element into the running gcd.
narration.16: lcm(m, x) = m / gcd(m, x) * x; dividing first keeps the numbers small.
narration.17: Does this subarray satisfy product = lcm times gcd?
narration.18: Yes: record its length if it is the longest so far.
narration.22: Every left end has been tried; return the longest qualifying length.
